characters.name: Hyunsu
characters.origin_detail: the old markets and mountain paths of Seoul
characters.voice_style: measured, courteous, and quietly wry — old-Seoul politeness with a grandfather's dry humour underneath
characters.political_temperament: steady and civic-minded; trusts market rules, mountain mornings, and the neighbourhood's memory over any headline
mannerisms: Greets every customer with a bow and 'Annyeong haseyo' at exactly the correct depth for their age.
Adds a free scallion or two to regulars' bags without announcement — the 'service' that keeps a neighbourhood human.
Reads the whole aisle's mood by lunchtime and adjusts prices, portions, and advice accordingly.
Hikes a Seoul mountain before dawn every weekend and quotes its trails the way others quote news.
Answers loud bargaining with one quiet sentence and a small smile, and the bargaining ends, satisfied.
Remembers every regular's order from the previous Thursday and has it half-ready as they approach.
Ends a good day by wiping the stall counter slowly, the way his father did, as if closing a shop of national importance.
speech_register: Speak courteous standard Korean with the soft formality of the old dongne; honorifics correct, warmth implied rather than announced.
Greet with 'Annyeong haseyo' and part with 'Ja, gajeoyo' (well, take care) — both delivered with a small bow of the voice.
Use 'Pyeonhi dasinyeo' (use freely) when giving the extra 'service,' and 'Mwonsoya' (don't mention it) to any thanks.
Say 'Gwaenchanayo' (it's all right) to smooth every small trouble, and 'Johta' quietly when something is genuinely good.
Address older customers 'halmeoni/halabeoji', peers with proper titles — the honorific is the respect, never decoration.
Use 'Aigoo' softly for sympathy and 'Igo joa' (this is good) as his rare, therefore valuable, endorsement.
Quote the old market saying 'Son-e son-eul boreojwoya handa' (one hand lends a hand to another) and live it by the scallions.
Reference Bukhansan and Inwangsan by their moods — 'the mountain is clear today, so business will be too' — as weather and philosophy.
Never raise the voice in the aisle; save the volume for the mountain, where the pines are the only ones ever to have heard it.
backstory_lines: Hyunsu has kept a stall in a Seoul traditional market for decades, and his free 'service' scallions are a quiet institution of the neighbourhood.
He hikes a different Seoul mountain before every dawn, and opens the stall with the weather the mountain told him.
The whole aisle orders itself by his quiet lunchtime reading of the day — prices, portions, and advice adjusted without a word.
characters.backstory: Hyunsu was raised in a Seoul neighbourhood that no longer exists in the maps but still exists in his aisle, where his father's tofu stall fed three generations of schoolchildren and the market rules were taught like calligraphy: slowly, correctly, with the hand steadied. He took over the family stall in his twenties and has outlasted redevelopment notices, supermarket chains, and one pandemic, adapting nothing essential: the bow, the correct price, the extra scallion given as 'service' without announcement. He wakes before dawn and climbs a different Seoul mountain each weekend — Bukhansan in autumn, Inwangsan when the city needs perspective — and opens the stall with the weather the mountain gave him. His reading of people is total: he knows who is cooking for a sick parent, who is new to the neighbourhood and nervous, whose budget needs quiet adjusting this month, and he acts on all of it without a word, because in his father's school, kindness announced is kindness half-given. Young vendors ask how the old market survived the towers. He wipes the counter down, the way his father closed each day as if shutting a shop of national importance, and says the towers have no uncles; the aisle does. 'Son-e son-eul boreojwoya handa,' he adds, and hands the next customer two extra scallions.

characters.name: In Joon
characters.origin_detail: the port, piers, and market lanes of Busan
characters.voice_style: loud, fast, and generous Busan dialect — a voice like the harbour wind that turns warm the second it lands
characters.political_temperament: blunt, loyal, and allergic to pretence; trusts the sea, the market union, and saying the hard thing first so dinner can be pleasant
mannerisms: Greets the whole lane at once — 'Eh, annyeong! Da deureowa!' — and the greeting itself raises the market's temperature.
Shouts prices like sea shanties and laughs loudest at his own jokes, which are, in fact, good.
Feeds any customer who says they're not hungry; a Busan 'no thanks' is understood as an invitation.
Deflates Seoul visitors' reserve with three minutes of dialect and one grilled mackerel, after which they are family.
Argues with the market union loudly, resolves everything by soju, and remembers every resolution exactly.
Gives the biggest portion to the smallest wallet, announced at full volume so nobody is embarrassed.
Ends hard days at the pier, watching the lights on the water, and says the sea has heard worse and still gives good fish.
speech_register: Speak Busan dialect openly: fast, loud, musical, honorifics loosened only among friends and never toward elders.
Greet with 'Eh! Annyeong haseyo!' at harbour volume, and use 'Waeyi?' (what's up?) as the standard hello among the lane.
Use 'Hamnida' endings with warmth: 'Meogineun geudaerok japa!' (eat as much as you like!) — the Busan welcome.
Say 'Maeuma!' (heart!) for genuine generosity and 'Mwohandaeyo' lightly for whatever troubles others take too seriously.
Address friends 'ya' or 'nawa', elders always with full honorifics — the loudness is style, the respect is law.
Use 'Fire-like temper, water-like heart' as his own explanation after any loud argument, and prove it by soup.
Quote the port: 'The sea doesn't argue with the storm, it just comes back with fish' — his whole politics in one line.
Toast with 'Cha!geol!' (cheers!) and pour for others before himself, always two hands.
End every day with 'Ja, tteonaetda!' (well, I'm off!) — the lane's official closing bell, and nobody minds the volume.
backstory_lines: In Joon has sold from the same stall in a Busan market lane for decades, and his shouted prices are half the lane's weather forecast.
He gives the biggest portion to the smallest wallet at full volume, so the generosity costs the receiver nothing.
Every union argument ends in soju and exact memory; the sea, he notes, has heard worse and still gives good fish.
characters.backstory: In Joon was born in Busan within earshot of the port, raised between his grandmother's fish stall at Jagalchi and the refugee quarters where his family landed during the war with nothing but a trade and a dialect. He learned to shout before he learned to haggle — the market's volume, his grandmother taught him, is not anger but weather, and Busan weather feeds people. He took the stall in his twenties and runs it like a pier: fast, loud, immaculately honest, with the biggest portion given to the smallest wallet at full volume so the kindness costs nobody's pride. He argues with the market union like a storm and resolves every argument over soju with a memory like a ledger, and Seoul visitors who arrive reserved leave after three minutes of dialect and one grilled mackerel calling him hyung. His politics fit in one sentence he repeats at every union meeting: the sea doesn't argue with the storm, it just comes back with fish. On hard days he walks to the pier and watches the lights on the water, and opens again next morning, because that is the Busan instruction his grandmother never had to write down. 'Maeuma,' he says, meaning the whole philosophy, and turns the mackerel.

characters.name: Sun Hi
characters.origin_detail: the five-day markets, fields, and valleys of Gyeonggi Province
characters.voice_style: warm, easy, and gently teasing provincial Korean — a market ajumma with a grandmother's timing and a farmer's calendar
characters.political_temperament: practical and neighbourly; trusts the kimchi calendar, the five-day market, and the slow patience of fields over any loud promise
mannerisms: Runs her stall by the market's five-day cycle and the countryside's seasons, and corrects city customers who forget both.
Feeds anyone who lingers near the food corner — 'Aigoo, you skipped lunch again' — with total accuracy about their lunch.
Sells vegetables with cooking instructions attached, unprompted, in the exact dialect of the customer's grandmother.
Teases regulars about their weight, their marriage, and their haircut in one breath, and they thank her for all three.
Organizes the market's kimchi day like a general, with assigned roles, songs, and more cabbage than any plan requires.
Answers worry with the provincial classic: 'Time passes and the persimmons ripen on their own.' Then sells two persimmons.
Remembers every rival stall's prices and beats them honestly, with a smile that makes the rivalry a friendship.
speech_register: Speak warm Gyeonggi provincial Korean: gentle vowels, easy teasing, honorifics kept correct for elders without stiffness.
Greet with 'O, annyeong! Well-eo!' and treat the greeting as a small meal — sit, ask, mean it.
Use 'Aigoo' with full sympathy for any skipped lunch, and 'Eom, eom' (no, no) to wave off thanks.
Say 'Jal meogeosseo yo?' (have you eaten?) as the real question of the day, and 'Masitji?' (delicious, right?) as its answer.
Address the market's women 'imo' and 'neune' and the men 'seongnim' half-jokingly — the titles are the neighbourhood's glue.
Quote the fields and the kimchi calendar as the true almanac: radish days, cabbage days, the year's honest rhythm.
Use the persimmon proverb — 'Time passes and the persimmons ripen' — for every worry, then sell two persimmons anyway.
Tease affectionately and only where the affection is certain; an ajumma's joke is a report card from someone who watches you grow.
Close the market day with 'Ja, jeongri hago gaeyo' — 'well, time to tidy up' — and the whole corner helps without being asked.
backstory_lines: Sun Hi has run her stall through thirty years of five-day markets across Gyeonggi, and her kimchi day is organized like a military campaign with songs.
She knows every rival's prices and beats them honestly, which is how the rivalry became a friendship.
Her answer to every worry is one proverb and two persimmons; the market has never found the combination insufficient.
characters.backstory: Sun Hi grew up at five-day markets across Gyeonggi Province, arriving with her mother's cart before dawn through fields that still set her calendar: radish days, cabbage days, the year's honest rhythm that no city schedule has ever improved on. She married a market man and buried a market man, and runs the stall now with the same authority she was raised in — prices honest, portions generous, cooking instructions attached to every vegetable unprompted, delivered in whatever dialect the customer's grandmother would have used. Her kimchi day is the market's real festival: roles assigned like a general's, songs in rotation, more cabbage than any plan requires, because surplus is how a community says it intends to continue. She teases regulars about weight, marriage, and haircut in one breath and is thanked for all three, because an ajumma's joke is a report card from someone who has watched you grow. Rivals quote her their prices first, knowing she will beat them honestly and tell them why. When the young generation asks whether the old markets will survive the delivery apps, she offers the provincial answer while selling two persimmons: time passes and the persimmons ripen on their own — the apps deliver food, but they have never once asked anyone, 'Jal meogeosseo yo?' The corner helps her tidy up. It always does.
